sections.title: Why a home CD will not delete

items.q: Why can't you erase the 'black history' on a household CD in a file manager?
items.a: The data is **pits and lands burned in concentric rings**, not magnetized bits. No commercial home burner rewrote that layer. Odd-shaped novelty discs still play if those rings are intact.

items.q: Does write-once mean the files are safe for decades?
items.a: **No.** Permanence was inferred from 'I cannot delete it.' Sun, scratches, ink, and a missing drive still kill the read. A 2000s burner was ~¥10,000; a Sony blank ~¥90.

items.q: Which face of a CD actually holds the data?
items.a: The **printed/label face**. The rainbow side has no pits. Storing the disc pretty-side-up puts data on the table. The video calls this 30 years of intuitive damage.

items.q: Why can a signature on the shiny side still make a disc unreadable?
items.a: The pits can survive. The ink **refracts the laser**, so lands and pits do not return a clean signal. Wiping the marker often restores the read. Paint on the label face is worse.

items.q: What is the least-wrong way to clean a scratched home disc?
items.a: **Not a shirt.** Dedicated cleaner, then polish for deep scratches (Kenny: ~20–30 minutes by hand). Domestic repair demand is family video, not movies.

items.q: What do most of Kenny's customers do after a successful restore?
items.a: They **copy to a USB stick and discard the disc**. No shelf, no player, no optical drive on the new PC.

items.q: What remains when optical discs lose tool value?
items.a: A **memory object**. The sleeve still recalls a story when the laser cannot. Sony stopping game discs and Netflix's DVD-rental start mark the same short childhood window.

items.q: What should you do with a drawer of old home discs?
items.a: **Protect the labeled face, clean, copy off, do not trust the original.** The 学而思 mid-roll is an ad. The argument is migrate-then-keep-the-story.
